name: Condy
workload: Single-machine TCP recv throughput, varying message sizes, single-shot and multi-shot io_uring modes, vs Asio, Epoll, raw liburing, Monoio, Compio; also 4KB random file read IOPS, channel messaging, coroutine spawn/switch microbenchmarks
claimed_speedup: Network recv single-shot: 2110 MB/s vs Epoll 1734 MB/s (~1.22x) and vs Asio 1588 MB/s (~1.33x); multi-shot 2610 MB/s vs raw io_uring 2560 MB/s; random-read IOPS 598K vs Monoio 310K (~2x) and vs libaio ~3x; channel throughput 15x over Asio; coroutine spawn 6.6x over Asio; coroutine switch 16x over Asio
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7945HX x16, SK Hynix HFS001TEJ9X115N NVMe SSD 1TB PCIe4, Linux Mint 22 Cinnamon, kernel 7.0.0-14-generic
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring); requires liburing >= 2.3; small young project with few stars; benchmark repo (condy-bench) is separate from main repo so numbers not reproduced inline
caveats: Compiler optimization flags not explicitly stated (only compiler version given); benchmark hosted as chart images (.png) referenced from docs/bench.md with numeric callouts in prose, not a raw data table; project itself very new/low adoption
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "coroutine io_uring" (found condy-cpp/condy), then opened docs/bench.md

name: uring_exec
workload: ping-pong network test, blocksize 16384 bytes, timeout 5s, varying thread count (2/4/8) and concurrent session count (10/100/1000)
claimed_speedup: 1.6x-4.3x GiB/s throughput over asio across thread/session combos, e.g. 4 threads/1000 sessions: 4.411 GiB/s (uring_exec) vs 1.275 GiB/s (asio) = ~3.5x; 2 threads/10 sessions: 3.409 vs 1.868 = ~1.8x
tradeoffs: Linux io_uring only; ports liburing onto C++26 std::execution (stdexec), so requires stdexec + liburing; asio comparison uses asio's own io_uring backend not epoll, so gain is from sender/receiver design not from switching kernel API; niche/experimental, single author benchmark, exact commit hashes pinned (uring_exec 22a6674, asio 62481a2) so numbers are reproducible but old snapshots
caveats: Single benchmark run reported (no repeated trials/variance given); author-run, not independently verified; project last updated 2026-05-01
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "coroutine io_uring" (found Caturra000/uring_exec), then opened README.md Benchmark section

name: Asio io_uring backend (ASIO_HAS_IO_URING)
workload: Single-threaded microbenchmark: 10000 iterations over 100 pipe descriptors, comparing Asio's epoll reactor vs its io_uring reactor on the same io_context code path
claimed_speedup: epoll: real 0m1.602s (user 0.563s, sys 1.039s); io_uring: real 0m1.158s (user 0.342s, sys 0.807s) -- about 1.4x faster wall-clock time (derived from page data), though io_uring adds extra kernel-worker-thread CPU usage not fully captured in these numbers
stars_or_usage: 6.2k stars; widely used C++ networking library (basis of Boost.Asio)
tradeoffs: Original single-threaded-only limitation and multi-threaded io_context instability under Linux 5.13 noted by maintainer at time of posting; io_uring backend now merged into asio mainline (io_uring_service.hpp etc. present) but is opt-in via ASIO_HAS_IO_URING; a third commenter (WSL2, kernel 5.10.102) reported epoll actually faster than io_uring in their environment, showing result is not universal
caveats: Numbers come from a first-party GitHub issue comment by asio's own maintainer, not a dedicated benchmark file; CPU model and compiler flags not stated; a different commenter's WSL2 run showed the opposite result (epoll faster), so the win is environment-dependent; capped at tier C per hard rules for a first-party claim with partial methodology
found_via: GitHub: gh api search/issues q=repo:chriskohlhoff/asio io_uring benchmark (issue #401 "any plans on io_uring support?")

name: F-Stack
workload: Nginx CPS (connection:close, small packet), RPS (keep-alive, small packet) and bandwidth (keep-alive, 3.7KB packet) tests comparing stock Nginx (kernel epoll, with and without smp_affinity/reuseport tuning) vs Nginx+F-Stack (DPDK kernel-bypass, FreeBSD userspace TCP/IP stack) on a 40GbE NIC
claimed_speedup: README states F-Stack/DPDK stack can sustain up to 10 million concurrent connections, 5 million RPS and 1 million CPS 'under full [NIC] load'; the CPS/RPS/Bandwidth comparison charts (CPS.png, RPS.png, Bandwidth.png) plot Nginx-epoll vs Nginx+F-Stack but the numeric axis values are embedded in images and could not be read as text, so an exact fold-improvement is not confirmed here
hardware: Intel XL710 40GbE NIC, Xeon E5-2670 v3 (NUMA), 128GB RAM, CentOS 7.2, kernel 3.10.104
license: NOASSERTION (repo shows license 'Other' on GitHub; F-Stack itself states BSD-style terms per component -- verify per-file before reuse)
stars_or_usage: 4.2k stars; used in production at Tencent Cloud (DNSPod, HttpDNS, CDN/COS access modules)
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK + hugepages + dedicated NIC (kernel bypass), not a drop-in for arbitrary apps; Linux/FreeBSD only; adds operational complexity (core pinning, ASLR disabling); ported FreeBSD 11/13 TCP stack so feature/behavior parity with Linux netstack is not perfect
caveats: Benchmark numbers exist only as chart images, not machine-readable text, so the exact speedup ratio could not be extracted or verified from the page; compiler and build flags for the nginx binaries are not stated; test environment (2016-era CPU) is old
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "F-Stack" (found F-Stack/f-stack), opened README Nginx Testing Result section

name: Monoio (additional Tier A benchmark vs epoll/asio, found via condy-bench)
workload: Single-machine TCP recv throughput at 2048B message size, single-shot mode, measured alongside Condy/Asio/Epoll/Compio on the same harness (condy-bench)
claimed_speedup: Monoio single-shot: 1887 MB/s vs Epoll 1734 MB/s (~1.09x) and vs Asio 1588 MB/s (~1.19x) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang 18.1.3 (flags not stated) for the C/C++ comparison points; Monoio itself built with its default Rust release profile (not separately stated in this doc)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7945HX x16, SK Hynix HFS001TEJ9X115N NVMe SSD 1TB PCIe4, Linux Mint 22 Cinnamon, kernel 7.0.0-14-generic
tradeoffs: Rust, not C++; benchmark run by a third-party project (condy) rather than monoio's own suite, so it is independent-ish but not peer reviewed; margin over epoll here is modest (~9%) compared to Condy's own bigger wins
caveats: This is supplemental Tier A evidence for an already-known project (monoio), surfaced incidentally while evaluating Condy's benchmark suite; per instructions, reported with is_evidence_for_known=true rather than as a new catalog candidate
found_via: GitHub: opened condy-cpp/condy docs/bench.md (same page as the Condy entry above)
